1289.title: On Patmos (Revelation 1:9–20)
1289.hook: John, exiled, sees the risen Christ among lampstands: fear not
1289.carry: fear not, I am the first
1289.howItsDone: Christians read this vision of the risen Christ in personal prayer and in church, and its words 'fear not; I am the first and the last' are read in times of grief and trouble.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Alpha and Omega: God holding the whole alphabet, A to Z. Your line was the beginning and the end.

"I John, who also am your brother, and companion in tribulation." That's how the man who saw all this introduces himself. Not as a prophet, not as a bishop. Your brother. Your companion in the hard part. Then he says where he is: "in the isle that is called Patmos, for the word of God, and for the testimony of Jesus Christ." An island, sea on every side. Tradition says he'd been banished. It's the Lord's day, he's in the Spirit, and from behind him comes a voice loud as a trumpet. Today, the moment John turns around.
screen: `A VOICE LIKE A TRUMPET, BEHIND HIM.`

segments.voice: First, he turns to see a voice. That's how the King James puts it: "And I turned to see the voice that spake with me. And being turned, I saw seven golden candlesticks." Lampstands, standing in the dark, and in the midst of them "one like unto the Son of man." Second, the figure. John piles up pictures, because ordinary words won't hold it. Hair white as wool, white as snow. Eyes like a flame of fire. Feet like polished brass glowing in a furnace. A voice like many waters. Seven stars in his right hand. A sharp two-edged sword from his mouth. A face like the sun at full strength. Not meant to be drawn like a photo; meant to overwhelm. Third, what John does, and what Christ does. "When I saw him, I fell at his feet as dead." Then the tender part: "he laid his right hand upon me, saying unto me, Fear not; I am the first and the last." The hand that holds the stars is laid on a frightened man. "I am he that liveth, and was dead; and, behold, I am alive for evermore." Fourth, the vision explains itself: "the seven candlesticks which thou sawest are the seven churches." So the first thing Revelation unveils about the risen Christ is where he stands. Not far off in the sky. In the midst of the churches, among the small, flickering lamps, with all their trouble. Present, not distant.

Name one thing you're afraid of at the moment, quietly, without arguing with it, then imagine a hand laid on you, warm and steady, as in the vision. If you pray, let the words come: Fear not; I am the first and the last; if not, just notice the steadiness of the hand. Each time the fear comes back, feel the hand again.
On Patmos. An island where John, companion in tribulation, saw the risen Christ standing among lampstands, and heard: fear not.
Your line: fear not, I am the first. Said with a hand laid on a frightened man. Rest easy.

1290.title: Ephesus (Revelation 2:1–7)
1290.hook: hard-working, but they've left their first love
1290.howItsDone: Christians read the letters to the seven churches as words to their own congregations, and some churches use the letter to Ephesus in retreats and renewal services that invite members to remember how their faith began.

segments.voice: Yesterday, on Patmos: John on the ground, and a right hand laid on him. Your line was fear not, I am the first.

A performance review lands on your desk. The first paragraph glows. You work hard. You don't give up. You've stood up to people who were lying to you. You've kept going when it was tiring, and you haven't fainted. Then the turn, in one word: nevertheless. That's roughly the shape of the first letter in Revelation, to the church in Ephesus. The lampstands from Patmos are about to get their mail, seven letters, one by one, and the first goes to a church that, on paper, is doing everything right.

First, who's writing: the risen Christ from the vision, who "holdeth the seven stars in his right hand, who walketh in the midst of the seven golden candlesticks." Walking among them. He knows these churches from the inside. Second, the praise, and it's real. "I know thy works, and thy labour, and thy patience." They've tested people who claimed to be apostles and found them liars. They've endured, and "for my name's sake hast laboured, and hast not fainted." Not a lazy church. Third, the turn: "Nevertheless I have somewhat against thee, because thou hast left thy first love." Left, not lost. Readers hear the first love more than one way. Some hear love for Christ himself, the warmth of the early days. Some hear love for one another, which can thin out in a church busy defending the truth. Some hear both, and the text doesn't choose. In this letter, hard work doesn't count as love on its own. A church can be right, busy and tired, and still have walked away from what started it. Fourth, the way back, in three steps: "Remember therefore from whence thou art fallen, and repent, and do the first works." Remember where it began. Repent: turn around. Do the first works: don't wait to feel it again; do what you did when you loved. And a promise that reaches back to Eden: "To him that overcometh will I give to eat of the tree of life, which is in the midst of the paradise of God."
screen: `NEVERTHELESS: THOU HAST LEFT THY FIRST LOVE.`

segments.voice: Think back to the start of something you still do, a faith, a friendship, a marriage, a job, a craft, and let one of its first works come into view: something you did back then, unasked, just because you loved it. If you pray, bring that memory to God; if not, hold it, and notice how far or how near it feels now.
Ephesus. The first of the seven churches: hard-working and enduring, and told it had left its first love, with a way back: remember, turn, do the first works.
Your line: your first love. Left, not lost, so the road back is still open. I'll be here tomorrow.

1291.title: Smyrna (Revelation 2:8–11)
1291.hook: poor but rich: be faithful unto death
1291.howItsDone: Christians who face poverty or persecution read the letter to Smyrna as words addressed to them, and 'be thou faithful unto death' is read and sung in churches as words of encouragement.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ephesus: a hard-working church told it had left its first love. Your line was your first love.

Four words in parentheses hold the heart of today's letter. The King James prints it like this: "I know thy works, and tribulation, and poverty, (but thou art rich)." A poor church, under pressure, about to face worse. And in the sentence that names their poverty, almost as an aside, a correction: but you're rich. The second letter goes to the church in Smyrna, and it differs from yesterday's in a way you could miss on a first read: in what isn't said.

First, who's speaking: "These things saith the first and the last, which was dead, and is alive." Of all the titles from the Patmos vision, this is the one chosen for Smyrna. To people who may face death, the writer has been through death and come out the other side. Second, poor but rich. Their poverty is real; the letter doesn't pretend otherwise. But it measures wealth in another currency, as Jesus does in the Gospels with treasure in heaven, where moth and rust don't reach. The parentheses are small, but they turn the sentence. Third, what's missing. Ephesus got praise and then nevertheless. Smyrna gets no nevertheless, no rebuke at all. Only comfort and a warning: "Fear none of those things which thou shalt suffer: behold, the devil shall cast some of you into prison, that ye may be tried; and ye shall have tribulation ten days." It doesn't promise escape. Some readers hear the ten days as a limit, and the letter's "I know" tells them they won't face it unseen. Fourth, the command and the gift: "be thou faithful unto death, and I will give thee a crown of life." Some readers note this crown is a victor's wreath, the kind given to someone who finishes a race, rather than a king's crown. Faithful unto death can mean to the point of dying. It can also mean all the way to the end of a life, one ordinary day after another. The letter closes: "He that overcometh shall not be hurt of the second death." The first death may come. The letter says the second will not hurt them.
screen: `THE ONE WHO WAS DEAD, AND IS ALIVE.`
`FAITHFUL UNTO DEATH: A CROWN OF LIFE.`

segments.voice: Think of one small promise nobody is checking on, a call you said you'd make, a habit you started, a person you said you'd look in on, and notice whether it feels heavy or light. Then choose to keep it today, just today. If you pray, ask for help to be faithful in that one thing; if not, just make the choice quietly.
Smyrna. The poor church called rich, given no rebuke, only courage: be faithful unto death, and a crown of life.
Your line: a crown of life. A wreath for the one who keeps going to the end. See you at the next letter.

1292.title: Pergamum (Revelation 2:12–17)
1292.hook: a white stone with a new name only you know
1292.howItsDone: Christians read the seven letters of Revelation 2–3 both as messages to real early churches and as words for churches today, and Bible study groups sometimes take them one letter at a time.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Smyrna: poor on paper, rich in the letter's eyes. Your line was a crown of life.

A small white stone. That's the gift at the end of today's letter, and the letter never says what it means. It goes to the church in Pergamum, a city the King James spells Pergamos. The risen Christ speaks as the one with the sharp sword with two edges, and his first words aren't a complaint. He knows their address: "where Satan's seat is." A hard place to live. Then, at the very end, the strange promise: a white stone, with a new name only the one who receives it knows.

First, where they lived. They "holdest fast my name, and hast not denied my faith." The letter names one man, Antipas, "my faithful martyr, who was slain among you." That's all the text says about him. What Satan's seat was, it doesn't say either. Some readers point to the city's great altars and temples; others to the worship of the emperor. Second, the trouble. Not everyone held the same line. The letter warns about some who held the teaching of Balaam, the hired prophet from Numbers, and others who held the teaching of the Nicolaitans. Faithful under pressure from outside, still muddled inside, and the letter says both. Third, the promise: "To him that overcometh will I give to eat of the hidden manna, and will give him a white stone, and in the stone a new name written, which no man knoweth saving he that receiveth it." Hidden manna reaches back to the bread in the wilderness. The white stone, readers have guessed at: a white pebble a juror cast to acquit, or a token that let a guest into a feast. The text doesn't explain. Fourth, the name. In the Bible, people are renamed at turning points: Abram becomes Abraham, Jacob becomes Israel, and Jesus calls Simon Peter. Here the new name isn't announced to the crowd. It's written on a stone and known only to the one who holds it. Others may know someone by a job, a reputation, a worst day. This letter says there's a name none of them gets to read.
screen: `A NEW NAME ONLY ONE PERSON KNOWS.`

segments.voice: Hold a small stone, or anything small and plain, in your palm, and feel its weight and edges as it warms. Let a question rest there without answering it in words: what would be written on it by someone who knew you all the way through, not your title, not your mistakes? If you pray, hold it and simply listen; if not, just hold it, and breathe.
Pergamum. A church holding fast in a hard place, warned about its muddle, and promised hidden manna and a white stone with a new name.
Your line: a new name. Written on a stone that nobody else gets to read. Until tomorrow.

1293.title: Thyatira (Revelation 2:18–29)
1293.hook: their latest works are more than their first
1293.howItsDone: Christians speak of growing in faith over a lifetime, and some make a habit of looking back over each day in prayer to notice what went well and what could be done better tomorrow.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Pergamum, and a white stone with a name on it that nobody else can read. Your line was a new name.

By a riverside outside the city of Philippi, Paul sits down with some women who have gathered to pray. One of them, Acts says, is "a certain woman named Lydia, a seller of purple, of the city of Thyatira." A businesswoman far from home. She listens, and the text says the Lord opened her heart. Her home town is today's word. Revelation's next letter goes to its church, and the voice is fierce: eyes "like unto a flame of fire," feet like fine brass. You'd brace for a scolding. Instead, the first thing he says is a compliment worth framing. This church is getting better.

First, the praise: "I know thy works, and charity, and service, and faith, and thy patience, and thy works; and the last to be more than the first." Charity is the King James word here for love. Ephesus heard that it had left its first love. Thyatira hears the reverse: what they do now is more than what they did at the start. Second, the trouble. They put up with a teacher the letter calls "that woman Jezebel, which calleth herself a prophetess." It doesn't give her real name. Jezebel reaches back to the queen in the book of Kings, wife of King Ahab, who served Baal. The complaint is about what she taught: eating food sacrificed to idols, and what the letter calls fornication. Even here there's patience: "I gave her space to repent." Third, a word to everyone who didn't follow that teaching: "I will put upon you none other burden. But that which ye have already hold fast till I come." No new load. Keep hold of what you've got. Fourth, the promise: "And I will give him the morning star," a light that shows before dawn. So Thyatira has a real problem in its middle, and still the first thing heaven says to it is that it's growing. The letter doesn't treat growth as a peak you hit at the start and slide down from. It can keep going, a little more each season.
screen: `I WILL GIVE HIM THE MORNING STAR.`

segments.voice: Let yesterday play back slowly and stop it at one ordinary moment you'd do a little differently: a short answer to someone, a meal eaten standing up, a chance to help that went by. Picture today's version, one notch better, done with a bit more care. If you pray, offer that moment to God and ask for help with it; if not, just hold the picture and breathe.
Thyatira. Lydia's home town, and the church told that its latest works were more than its first, even with a real problem in its middle.
Your line: more than at first. Growth doesn't have to peak at the start. Go gently.

1294.title: Sardis (Revelation 3:1–6)
1294.hook: you have a name for being alive, but wake up
1294.howItsDone: Christians use the language of watchfulness and waking up in sermons and prayers, and some churches read the Gospel warnings to keep watch in Advent.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Thyatira: a church whose latest works were more than its first. Your line was more than at first.

A cliff so steep the guards didn't bother watching it. That's the story the old Greek historian Herodotus tells about the citadel of Sardis: an enemy soldier saw a defender climb down the rock to fetch a fallen helmet, noticed the way up nobody was guarding, and the city fell. Some readers hear that story behind today's letter; others say it needs no backstory. Either way, its opening lands like an alarm. The risen Christ tells the church in Sardis: everyone thinks you're alive. You aren't. Wake up.

First, the verdict, in the King James words: "I know thy works, that thou hast a name that thou livest, and art dead." A name for being alive: a good reputation, a full calendar, people who'd say this church is thriving. Notice what's missing. No persecution named, no false teacher. Just a church asleep inside its own good name. Second, what to do: "Be watchful, and strengthen the things which remain, that are ready to die." Not start over. Like a fire nearly out: you don't build a new one, you blow on the embers still red. Then: "Remember therefore how thou hast received and heard, and hold fast, and repent." Go back to how it began. Third, the warning: "If therefore thou shalt not watch, I will come on thee as a thief, and thou shalt not know what hour I will come upon thee." It echoes Jesus in the Gospels: "Watch therefore: for ye know not what hour your Lord doth come." A thief doesn't send a calendar invite. Fourth, the tender part: "Thou hast a few names even in Sardis which have not defiled their garments; and they shall walk with me in white." Even in a sleeping church, some are awake, and the letter counts them. And whoever overcomes, their name will not be blotted out of the book of life. So Sardis sets two names side by side: the name a church has with everyone else, and the name kept in the book of life. The letter cares about the second.

Choose something right around you that you've stopped noticing, the sound of the room, the weight of your hands, the light on a wall, and meet it as if for the first time. When your mind drifts back to sleep, and it will, wake up to it again; that's all watchfulness is, one return at a time. If you pray, ask to be kept awake; if not, just keep returning.
Sardis. The church with a name for being alive, told to wake up and strengthen what remains, with a few in white who never fell asleep.
Your line: wake up. The embers are still red, and there's something left to blow on. That's today.

1295.title: Philadelphia (Revelation 3:7–13)
1295.hook: little strength, but an open door no one can shut
1295.howItsDone: Christians sometimes speak of an 'open door' when a new chance to serve or to share their faith appears, borrowing the language of Revelation 3:8 and of Paul's letters.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sardis: a name for being alive, and a call to wake up. Your line was wake up.

"Thou hast a little strength." An odd line for a letter of praise. Not great strength, not hidden reserves. A little. That's what the risen Christ says to the church in Philadelphia, and not as a scolding. In the same breath he tells them a door has been set open in front of them, and nobody can shut it. A small church, low on strength, in front of a door it didn't open and can't be locked out of. It's the week's end, so the letters so far get a look back too.

First, who's speaking: "he that hath the key of David, he that openeth, and no man shutteth; and shutteth, and no man openeth." It echoes Isaiah, where a steward is handed the key of the house of David: "so he shall open, and none shall shut." The key isn't the church's. Second, the door: "behold, I have set before thee an open door, and no man can shut it: for thou hast a little strength, and hast kept my word, and hast not denied my name." The door isn't a prize for being strong. It's set open for people with a little strength who kept going. What the door is, readers differ. Some hear a door for sharing the gospel, as Paul writes that "a great door and effectual is opened unto me." Others hear the door into God's kingdom. Third, a promise for people who feel small: "Him that overcometh will I make a pillar in the temple of my God, and he shall go no more out." A pillar holds a building up and never gets moved out. Fourth, the week. It opened on Patmos with fear not. Ephesus was asked to return to its first love. Smyrna, poor but rich, was promised a crown of life. Pergamum got a white stone and a new name. Thyatira grew, more than at first. Sardis was told to wake up. Philadelphia, with its little strength, got a door. In the King James text, each letter turns to its church with the same words: I know thy works. Someone is paying attention to these churches.
